units.translation: ⟦1⟧ can actually be understood. He now shows awareness of his superiority; he and Athena belong together as children of Zeus, the new and better ruler, and from the reference to Pallas he turns directly to her. The gap before 665 seems clear, because of ⟦2⟧ and Aeschylus. ⟦3⟧ because in fact something more than the single v. 665 is required here; on the other hand, that 663 ⟦4⟧ stands without an expressed contrast (⟦5⟧) does not compel the assumption of a second (Weil) after 666. Rather, if it continued after 666: ⟦6⟧ (this is the sense Weil wants, see ⟦7⟧), that would tear apart a close connection.

looks like a captatio, but is addressed to the presiding goddess and not to the Areopagus, and is meant to emphasize the harmonious cooperation of the two deities. At the same time the conclusion of the speech is clearly marked, as with an epilogue, and accordingly Athena now closes the proceedings. If one has seen an argument ⟦1⟧ in the verses and recalled that such were forbidden before the Areopagus (cf. on 674), there is still a long way from that to deleting verses 667–673 as an insertion made at a revival after Aeschylus's death (so Weil). Ending at 666, Apollo's defense would be without any conclusion. — 667

⟦1⟧ has rightly been changed by Robortellus to ⟦2⟧, because it contradicts 708; that Athena does not want to force a conclusion but only proposes it is clearly shown by 678. Kirchhoff and Weil even make the sentence a complaint, and ⟦3⟧ into the subjunctive. Athena may indeed actually follow the custom of the Areopagus, allowing nothing ⟦4⟧, by cutting it off immediately.
